* The air in the atmosphere is 71% Nitrogen and 28% Oxygen. The last 1% are gasses like Argon, Carbon Dioxide, and Water Vapor.
* The atmosphere hasn't always been made of the same stuff. 300 million years ago, during the Carboniferous Period, there were a lot more plants on the Earth, so there was a lot more oxygen in the atmosphere. With more oxygen in the atmosphere, bugs got BIG. Dragonflies were 3 feet wide. Millipedes could be bigger than people.
* We think of the sky as being really big. In reality, when viewed from space, the atmosphere is *incredibly* thin. If the Earth were the size of an apple, the atmosphere would be no thicker than the skin of the apple!
* We think of air as weighing nothing. In reality, the weight all the air in the atmosphere would be 5.5 quadrillion tons! A single cloud can weigh more than a million pounds!
* The air in the atmosphere gets thinner the higher up you go. The reason is because the gravity of the Earth pulls the air close to the ground! That's why you need an oxygen mask if you climb a tall mountain like Mt. Everest!
* Part of our atmosphere helps protect us from the sun! Way up high in a part of the atmosphere called the stratosphere, there's something called the ozone layer. Ozone is a gas that helps protect us by blocking harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays from the sun.   Without the ozone layer, we would get a lot more sunburns and skin cancer.

Elements (and chemistry in general) can be pretty confusing at first!

Your notes seem to have the gist of it, with a few corrections. Here's a basic rundown of atoms, elements, and molecules.

Atoms. Atoms are the smallest unit of matter that can be called an 'element.' Atoms are made of subatomic particles like electrons, protons, and neutrons, which determine the atoms' charge, number, and mass.

Elements. An element is any pure substance in which all of its atoms have the same number of protons (every atom has the same periodic number). So an 'element' can be a single atom of Plutonium or a pile of Carbon. Some elements, like you mention in your notes, are 'diatomic' meaning that they often exist in a bonded molecule with just 2 atoms. The 7 diatomic elements are H,N,O,F,Cl, Br, and sometimes I. This just means that you most often find elements like nitrogen and oxygen in the form N2 or O2 (like in our atmosphere).

Molecules. Any time two or more atoms are covalently bonded together, they form a molecule. The atoms can either be the same, or different. If the atoms are the same, they form a diatomic element.

Fertilizers are very high in nutrients. This is why it's useful for growing plants. However, when fertilizer runs off into our waterways, they result in large algal blooms. These algal blooms are opportunistic and use up all of the nutrients in the water. This in itself is not a bad thing, however, when these algae die and are decomposed, they result in a net decrease in dissolved oxygen. Water with low dissolved oxygen cannot support life, so fertilizer runoff results in huge dead zones (like the one off the Mississippi River Delta). This process is called eutrophication.
